problems.description: GET /tasks is specified as ordered by created_at desc but test_list_tasks compares a set of titles, so ordering is never asserted.
tempfile.mkstemp leaves the original fd open while SQLite opens the same path; the app's -journal/-wal companion files (if any) are not cleaned up at teardown.

strengths: Comprehensive coverage of every session-1 requirement: POST/GET/PUT endpoints, 400 on missing title, 404 on not found, and JSON error shapes all asserted.
Per-test isolation via a temp SQLite database and Flask's TESTING/test_client idiom.
Goes beyond the spec by covering the blank-title edge case.
Clear, requirement-mapping test names and self-contained fixture.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, spec-aligned pytest suite for the task-manager API with proper per-test DB isolation, minor gaps only around ordering assertions and temp-file hygiene.

problems.description: Migration adds owner_id as NULL to pre-existing task rows, silently orphaning them: get_tasks/get_task now filter WHERE owner_id = ?, so existing tasks become invisible to every user after upgrade. No data backfill or ownership assignment strategy is defined.
JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-change-me' value, acceptable locally but a footgun if deployed without the env var; also no clock-skew leeway on exp.
JWT sub claim holds an int user id though the JWT spec (RFC 7519) defines sub as a string; PyJWT tolerates it but it is a common interop deviation.
No tests added for the new auth flow (register/login/401 paths, ownership isolation), while the story baseline ships without a test suite; leaves the new security-critical paths unverified.
Mixed datetime usage: legacy datetime.utcnow() retained in create_task while generate_token correctly uses datetime.now(timezone.utc); utcnow is deprecated in Python 3.12.

strengths: Preserves the single-file structure and section-header conventions (── Models/Auth/──) with snake_case, type-hinted model functions and the same get_db context-manager pattern.
Authorization enforced at the data-access layer: get_task, get_tasks, and update_task all filter by owner_id, preventing IDOR-style cross-user access rather than relying on route-level checks alone.
Idempotent migration via PRAGMA table_info that works for both fresh and pre-existing databases.
Secure credential handling: werkzeug password hashing and JWT with expiry; login_required returns consistent 401 responses for missing/invalid/expired tokens.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent Session 2 feature addition that cleanly extends the existing single-file Flask structure with per-user JWT auth and owner-scoped task access, with only minor concerns around orphaned pre-existing data, a dev-default secret, and missing tests.

problems.description: create_user silently fabricates a default email ({username}@example.com) for every user instead of making the field optional and handling None downstream, inventing data that has no real meaning.

Legacy users (pre-email) have NULL email; completing a task then calls send_notification_email.delay(g.user["email"], ...) with None, producing 'To: None' notifications. The migration test even asserts email stays NULL, yet no guard/backfill exists on the send path.

celery_config.py uses lowercase module-level names (broker_url, task_serializer, etc.), which is idiomatic Celery config but is flagged by the repo's convention checker (module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE) — the commit_analysis findings elsewhere in the repo flag this same pattern.
edit_task fetches previous_task via get_task before update_task, but update_task already re-fetches the task internally, adding a redundant DB read on every update.

strengths: Adds a clean async seam: celery_config.py supports task_always_eager via env var so tests and CI run in-process without a Redis broker.
The email migration mirrors the existing owner_id ALTER TABLE pattern (PRAGMA table_info check + conditional ALTER), so it degrades gracefully on legacy DBs.
Notification is fired only on a status transition (pending -> completed), not on repeated updates to an already-completed task.
Broker/backend/task_routes are env-overridable, keeping the config deployment-agnostic.
Strong test coverage: email default, custom email, trigger assertion via mock delay, and a failure-isolation test for the non-blocking requirement.
commit_reviews.summary: Faithfully implements the mandated Celery/Redis notification spec with good tests and an eager-mode test seam, but carries minor debt from a fabricated default email, an unguarded None-email path for legacy users, and a convention-tooling clash over lowercase Celery config.

problems.description: Gratuitous import reorder in app.py: `from datetime import timedelta, timezone, datetime` breaks alphabetical ordering that the previous `datetime, timedelta, timezone` had, adding diff noise for no benefit.
BaseRepository.delete is defined but never called by any route or test — speculative dead code in a refactor whose goal was extracting only what routes need.

Mixed entry points: login_required calls user_repository.find_by_id directly while the login/register routes go through the kept `get_user_by_username` 'backwards compatibility' wrapper — an inconsistency in a single-module codebase with no external consumers.
repositories.cpython-310.pyc is committed alongside the source (systemic harness behavior across story commits, but it is noise in this diff).

strengths: Fully satisfies the session 4 requirement: all SQL extracted from route handlers into BaseRepository/UserRepository/TaskRepository; routes touch no cursors or query strings.
Connection-factory injection — `get_db` passed by reference into module-level repository singletons — is a clean test seam and stays correct if DATABASE is reassigned.
Behavior-preserving refactor: owner-scoping preserved everywhere (find_by_id_for_owner, list_for_owner, update's WHERE id AND owner_id), so no authorization regression.
Verified: all 38 existing tests pass with zero modifications (confirmed by re-running pytest at this commit).
Follows repo conventions: PascalCase classes, snake_case methods, type hints on public signatures, documented design decisions in comments.
commit_reviews.summary: A behavior-preserving, well-architected repository-pattern refactor that fully meets the session 4 spec and passes all 38 tests, with only minor convention noise (import reorder, unused delete, a vestigial compat wrapper).

problems.description: flask-limiter is imported and wired into app.py but no requirements.txt entry appears in the diff, leaving a new runtime dependency undeclared and the app non-reproducible outside the instrumented environment.
list_tasks ordering silently changes from created_at DESC (the previous contract) to id ASC for cursor stability; the first page is now oldest-first, a behavioral change no test asserts either way.

The Limiter hard-defaults to redis://localhost:6379/0 with no in-memory fallback or swallow_errors; tests rely on limiter.reset() but will error the moment Redis is unavailable, coupling the whole suite to an external service.
Type inconsistency in the cursor contract: cursor arrives as int but next_cursor is returned as str(rows[-1]["id"]), exposing raw row ids rather than an opaque cursor.
rate_limit_key only catches jwt.PyJWTError; a token signed with the app's own secret but missing the 'sub' claim raises KeyError and 500s instead of falling back to the IP key.

strengths: Keyset cursor pagination is pushed into the repository layer with a limit+1 fetch so next_cursor is only set when a next page truly exists
User-aware rate-limit keys (JWT subject) with IP fallback let one default_limits cover both authenticated task endpoints and unauthenticated auth endpoints as the story requires
Type-hinted public signatures and module-level env constants (RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI, DEFAULT_PAGE_LIMIT, MAX_PAGE_LIMIT) match the codebase's conventions
429 responses return the same JSON error shape as the rest of the API, and existing list tests were updated to the new {data, next_cursor, total} envelope
New pagination tests cover the empty page, default page size of 20, and cursor walk to the next page; limiter.reset() in the fixture keeps tests independent
commit_reviews.summary: Competently adds Redis-backed Flask-Limiter rate limiting (user-keyed with IP fallback) and id-keyset cursor pagination kept in the repository layer with updated and new tests, but ships an undeclared flask-limiter dependency and a silent ordering/response-contract change that constitute the main debt.

compounding_issues: Unconstrained status field (session 1 accepted any string) left two competing vocabularies — tests used 'done' while the session 3 notification trigger only fires on 'completed', so the async email silently never fires for clients using 'done'.

Session 2's owner_id scoping decision was baked into every query and API contract, so all later sessions (and the session 5 response-envelope change) were forced to ripple through the data-access layer.

Redis became a hard runtime dependency: Celery (session 3) and Flask-Limiter (session 5) both default to redis://localhost:6379/0, and the session 5 test suite had to add per-fixture limiter.reset() to stay independent of cross-test Redis state.
Hardcoded default JWT_SECRET 'dev-secret-change-me' from session 2 was carried through to the final commit as unresolved security debt.

Session 5 changed the list_tasks response envelope, forcing retroactive edits to pre-existing tests (test_list_tasks, test_users_only_see_their_own_tasks) — expected churn, but a sign the public shape wasn't locked down earlier.
key_decisions: Session 1: single-file Flask app with function-per-model seams and raw SQLite, deliberately structured as 'tier 1 good seams' so later sessions could extend without a rewrite.

Session 2: adding per-user ownership (owner_id) plus JWT auth with in-place PRAGMA-based ALTER TABLE migrations in init_db — the migration pattern kept the same codebase evolvable across sessions without data loss.
Session 3: introducing Celery for async email notifications behind a task_always_eager env toggle, keeping the integration testable without a live broker.

Session 4: extracting a repository layer (BaseRepository + UserRepository/TaskRepository, all SQL moved out of app.py) — the single most enabling choice, making session 5's pagination and rate limiting clean additions.
Session 5: cursor-based pagination with a next_cursor envelope plus Flask-Limiter keyed per-user-or-IP with a shared 429 handler.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality steadily improved across the five sessions. Session 1 delivered a clean baseline with immediate test coverage; session 2 was the largest jump, adding auth and per-user isolation with thoughtful migration handling that kept the seed data model extensible; session 3 integrated async notifications with a sensible eagerness toggle for testability; session 4 raised the architecture by extracting a repository layer and shrinking app.py by over half; session 5 capped the arc with cursor pagination and rate limiting, backed by the largest and most thorough test expansion (53 passing tests, run twice to rule out Redis-state flakiness). The only sustained blemishes were small and inherited — a loose status enum, a hardcoded dev JWT secret, and a growing Redis dependency — none of which ever broke a session.
